Title: Solar Eclipses and the Saros Cycle
Content: Solar eclipses occur between `text(two)` and `text(five)` times a `text(year)` somewhere on `text(Earth)`, but are rare for any `text(one)` location. The plane of the `text(Moon's)` orbit is tilted approximately `5°` to `text(Earth's)` orbit around the `text(Sun)`. So, even though the `text(Moon)` is in the correct phase, `text(New Moon)`, to produce a solar eclipse, the `text(Moon's)` shadow usually falls above or below `text(Earth's)` position in its orbit. To produce a total solar eclipse, the `text(Moon)` in its orbit must be at or near its closest point to `text(Earth)`, making it appear large enough to cover the `text(Sun)`. Solar eclipses follow specific, cyclic patterns called Saros Cycles. A Saros Cycle lasts `text(18 years)`, `text(11 days)`, and `text(8 hours)`. Since `text(eight hours)` is approximately `text(one-third)` of `text(Earth's daily)` rotation, it takes `text(three)` Saros Cycles (`text(54 years)` and `text(34 days)`) for a solar eclipse to return to the same section of `text(Earth)`.
